external_evidence.applicability: Helps define how to check systemic symptoms and splenomegaly. Does not prove lymphoma or its subtype; the list of lymphoma workups does not make all invasive procedures mandatory in unexplained fever.
external_evidence.proposition: Assessing suspected lymphoma combines a history of systemic symptoms, examination of nodes and spleen, a complete blood count with morphology and imaging. Diagnosis usually requires a biopsy of the relevant lesion before treatment.
external_evidence.title: JSH practical guidelines for hematological malignancies, 2023: II. lymphoma—overview

external_evidence.applicability: Supports only a conditional branch with a corresponding cellular and anatomical pattern. Mild splenomegaly and hemoglobin 121 g/L do not by themselves indicate this subtype or justify splenectomy.
external_evidence.proposition: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma requires morphological and immunophenotypic data. Some cases can be recognized by clonal small B cells in blood and/or bone marrow after excluding other small B-cell neoplasms. A negative PET-CT does not exclude marginal zone lymphoma.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Guidelines Version 4.2026: Splenic Marginal Zone Lymphoma

external_evidence.applicability: Applicable once a suitable focus for biopsy appears. The available temperature up to 38°C and night sweats do not automatically warrant attributing the formal B-symptom complex or a Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis.
external_evidence.proposition: If Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected, a diagnostically adequate node biopsy, usually excisional, is preferred; fine-needle aspiration alone is usually insufficient. FDG uptake may be infectious or inflammatory and needs clinical or pathological clarification.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Guidelines Version 2.2026: Hodgkin Lymphoma

external_evidence.applicability: Clarifies the meaning of the known antibiotic exposure and the missing cultures/echocardiography. The time of intake and blood collection are unknown; there are no culture results, so calling the case proven culture-negative endocarditis is premature. The source does not justify exclusion by procalcitonin.

external_evidence.proposition: Antibiotics before blood collection are a common cause of negative cultures in endocarditis. With clinical suspicion, proper culture sets and valve assessment are needed; further pathogen search depends on exposures, prior antibiotics and primary results. Negative cultures after antibiotics do not exclude infection.
external_evidence.title: Blood Culture–Negative Endocarditis: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association

external_evidence.applicability: Allows choosing a check once a contact or focus is established. There is currently no material, exposures or tuberculosis tests; this is not a recommendation for invasive sampling without a clinical target.
external_evidence.location: Prose-only full text; exact BioC source retained
external_evidence.proposition: IGRA and the tuberculin test do not distinguish latent infection from active tuberculosis. If an extrapulmonary process is suspected, material from the relevant focus is examined: culture, molecular methods and, if indicated, histology. Negative results of a single test may not exclude disease.
external_evidence.title: Official American Thoracic Society/Infectious Diseases Society of America/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children

external_evidence.applicability: Supports the sequence for checking the systemic condition. The stated temperature “up to 38°C” does not document the temperature threshold of classic fever of unknown origin; objective inflammatory markers still need explanation. This is not a specialized guideline on spondylodiscitis, abscess or laboratory error.
external_evidence.location: Prose-only full text; exact BioC source retained
external_evidence.proposition: Unexplained fever and unexplained inflammation have infectious, non-infectious inflammatory, neoplastic and other causes. The initial assessment includes history, examination, a blood count with differential and inflammatory markers. FDG PET-CT may localize a focus for a directed check after a non-diagnostic initial workup; FDG uptake does not determine etiology.
external_evidence.title: EANM consensus document on the use of [18F]FDG PET/CT in fever and inflammation of unknown origin

external_evidence.applicability: Age 55 and inflammation allow clarifying relevant symptoms but do not establish vasculitis by themselves. Clinical suspicion, operator experience and the effect of glucocorticoids already received change the interpretation of results; no treatment is prescribed here.
external_evidence.location: Official publisher HTML text; use overarching principles and Recommendation 1-3 prose only, no protocol table/image claims.
external_evidence.proposition: With clinical suspicion of giant cell arteritis, initial imaging may be expert ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries; the choice of alternative imaging depends on the region and availability. Strong suspicion with ischemic visual manifestations requires urgent clinical action without waiting for a planned study.
external_evidence.title: EULAR recommendations for the use of imaging in large vessel vasculitis in clinical practice: 2023 update.

external_evidence.applicability: ANA 1:320 justifies an organ-directed assessment, but the method and specific manifestations are unknown. By the description of up to 38°C the temperature criterion is not met; this does not exclude lupus. Unknown organ results are not counted as negative.
external_evidence.location: Physical PDF pages 5, 7, 8: clinical definitions, final classification criteria, discussion
external_evidence.proposition: ANA are an entry condition for lupus classification, not a standalone diagnosis. Clinical and immunological features without a better alternative explanation are needed; classification criteria do not replace diagnosis. The temperature criterion is above 38.3°C; with high C-reactive protein, infection must be considered.
external_evidence.title: 2019 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus

external_evidence.applicability: A temperature up to 38°C does not match the typical description of spikes; rash, blood differential and ferritin are unknown. The section on macrophage activation syndrome signals a need to assess hyperinflammation but is not a full algorithm for secondary HLH in lymphoma or infection.
external_evidence.location: Paragraph-only full-body derivative; exact source XML retained. Tables, figures and supplementary material excluded.
external_evidence.proposition: The Still profile includes typical temperature spikes ≥39°C, a transient rash, musculoskeletal manifestations and inflammatory activity; arthritis is not mandatory. Infections, tumors and other inflammatory diseases need to be considered. In a rheumatic context, the combination of persistent fever, splenomegaly, rising ferritin, low cell counts, liver/coagulation abnormalities or triglycerides requires assessment for macrophage activation syndrome; any single feature is non-specific.
external_evidence.title: EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still’s disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still’s disease

external_evidence.applicability: Meropenem and vancomycin document exposure but not its causation. The entire medication chronology is needed, including drugs before April; the available description does not establish the start date of each agent. The review does not replace a severe drug reaction protocol.
external_evidence.location: Body prose: definition, clinical presentation and diagnosis; tables excluded
external_evidence.proposition: Drug fever requires temporal matching with exposure, assessment of other causes and the course after stopping the drug. The review uses a working definition with regression within 72 hours but notes that definitions vary. Re-challenge is not a safe universal confirmation.
external_evidence.title: Drug fever: a narrative review

external_evidence.applicability: IgA 0.06 g/L is a reason to reassess immunoglobulins. A single undated result is insufficient. The page does not contain the full CVID criteria pathway, so this diagnosis is not established.
external_evidence.location: Physical PDF page 45: Selective IgA deficiency working criteria
external_evidence.proposition: The working definition of selective IgA deficiency requires more than low IgA: clinical/family context, repeat IgA together with IgG and IgM, exclusion of secondary causes, a preserved IgG vaccine response and exclusion of a T-cell defect are considered.
external_evidence.title: ESID Registry – Working Definitions for Clinical Diagnosis of PID, November 2019

external_evidence.applicability: Applicable to the described left nodule. Size, ultrasound features and TSH are unknown; no automatic puncture or causal link to the fever is established. Exact thresholds from the tables were not used.
external_evidence.location: Body prose: initial evaluation, clinical and laboratory evaluation, ultrasound; tables/figures excluded
external_evidence.proposition: The initial assessment of a thyroid nodule includes history, examination, TSH and neck ultrasound. The need for puncture is determined after clinical, functional and ultrasound assessment, taking risk and size into account.
external_evidence.title: 2023 European Thyroid Association Clinical Practice Guidelines for thyroid nodule management

external_evidence.applicability: The historical alternative is kept separate from lymphoma. There is no full node assessment or histology, so the major criteria are unchecked rather than proven absent. The subtype is not established; the table is part 1 of 2 and is not used as a complete finished algorithm.
external_evidence.proposition: Criteria for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease require both major features: corresponding node histology and node enlargement in at least two regions; minor criteria and exclusion of mimics are also required. Inflammation, anemia and splenomegaly alone are insufficient; autoantibodies alone are not an exclusion.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Guidelines Version 2.2026: Castleman Disease

external_evidence.applicability: Used to limit the historical branch of aggressive B-cell lymphoma: morphology of a suspicious focus is needed first. Staging and pre-treatment assessment studies are not automatically transferred to undiagnosed fever.
external_evidence.proposition: The workup for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma includes anatomical assessment of nodes and organs, blood differential, LDH and imaging. Bone marrow biopsy is listed among studies for selected cases; this section is not a way to establish a subtype from systemic symptoms alone.
external_evidence.title: NCCN Guidelines Version 4.2026: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma

items.body: Fever since April 2026, night sweats, mild splenomegaly on CT of 16.04.2026 and the inflammatory syndrome are compatible with lymphoma, but also with infection and non-infectious inflammation. Hemoglobin 121 g/L on 31.07.2026 does not determine the cause of anemia. LDH 410.8 U/L and β₂-microglobulin 2.28 mg/L are given without dates or reference intervals; they neither establish nor exclude lymphoma. There is no description of lymph nodes, weight loss, blood smear or histology. The lymphoma type and check priority are currently undetermined.

items.body: Prolonged fever, night sweats, splenomegaly and high C-reactive protein values allow for an endovascular infectious source. The history mentions meropenem and vancomycin, but there is no time of prescription, blood cultures, echocardiography or description of the response. The wording about an undetermined cause of fever proves neither treatment failure nor absence of infection. An undated procalcitonin of 0.06 ng/mL cannot be matched to the C-reactive protein peak or used to exclude endocarditis.

CT of 16.04.2026 preceded the highest value given; a list of several findings does not confirm a full exclusion of a focus. items.body: Fever, inflammatory syndrome and splenomegaly can occur in adult-onset Still disease, but the available description has substantial mismatches and gaps: temperature is given only as “up to 38°C”, ANA are positive at 1:320, and there is no description of the typical rash, arthralgias, sore throat, neutrophilic differential or ferritin. Leukocytes of 8.25×10⁹/L on 31.07.2026 do not document neutrophilic leukocytosis during peak inflammatory activity. This is an unconfirmed alternative for clarifying the phenotype, with no priority over infectious or neoplastic explanations.

Their causal link to the fever and inflammatory markers is not shown. items.body: The source wording “fever of unknown origin” coexists with a temperature of only “up to 38°C”; it should be kept, but formal fulfillment of the syndrome criteria still needs checking. C-reactive protein 673.1 mg/L is kept verbatim; the extreme value is a reason to reconcile the primary form, unit and repeat measurements, not to correct the number independently. The dates of procalcitonin, ANA, ANCA, IgA, Anti-CCP, CMV PCR, LDH, β₂-microglobulin, PSA, uric acid and AST/ALT 24 U/L are unknown. In the biochemistry of 31.07.2026, units and reference intervals are not given for AST 15.96, ALT 10, GGT 15.4, ALP 70.3, direct bilirubin 1.37, urea 5.18, creatinine 79.95, glucose 4.98 and total protein 70.88. Erythrocytes of 4.86×10¹²/L do not replace red cell indices. These circumstances do not refute the disease but prevent conclusions about normality, simultaneity of tests or treatment effect.

items.body: Assessing suspected lymphoma combines a history of systemic symptoms, examination of nodes and spleen, a complete blood count with morphology and imaging. Diagnosis usually requires a biopsy of the relevant lesion before treatment. Application to the case: Helps define how to check systemic symptoms and splenomegaly. Does not prove lymphoma or its subtype; the list of lymphoma workups does not make all invasive procedures mandatory in unexplained fever.

items.body: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma requires morphological and immunophenotypic data. Some cases can be recognized by clonal small B cells in blood and/or bone marrow after excluding other small B-cell neoplasms. A negative PET-CT does not exclude marginal zone lymphoma. The workup for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma includes anatomical assessment of nodes and organs, blood differential, LDH and imaging. Bone marrow biopsy is listed among studies for selected cases; this section is not a way to establish a subtype from systemic symptoms alone. Application to the case: Supports only a conditional branch with a corresponding cellular and anatomical pattern. Mild splenomegaly and hemoglobin 121 g/L do not by themselves indicate this subtype or justify splenectomy. Application to the case: Used to limit the historical branch of aggressive B-cell lymphoma: morphology of a suspicious focus is needed first. Staging and pre-treatment assessment studies are not automatically transferred to undiagnosed fever.

items.body: If Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected, a diagnostically adequate node biopsy, usually excisional, is preferred; fine-needle aspiration alone is usually insufficient. FDG uptake may be infectious or inflammatory and needs clinical or pathological clarification. Application to the case: Applicable once a suitable focus for biopsy appears. The available temperature up to 38°C and night sweats do not automatically warrant attributing the formal B-symptom complex or a Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis.

items.body: Antibiotics before blood collection are a common cause of negative cultures in endocarditis. With clinical suspicion, proper culture sets and valve assessment are needed; further pathogen search depends on exposures, prior antibiotics and primary results. Negative cultures after antibiotics do not exclude infection. Application to the case: Clarifies the meaning of the known antibiotic exposure and the missing cultures/echocardiography. The source does not justify exclusion by procalcitonin.

items.body: IGRA and the tuberculin test do not distinguish latent infection from active tuberculosis. items.body: Unexplained fever and unexplained inflammation have infectious, non-infectious inflammatory, neoplastic and other causes. The initial assessment includes history, examination, a blood count with differential and inflammatory markers. FDG PET-CT may localize a focus for a directed check after a non-diagnostic initial workup; FDG uptake does not determine etiology. Application to the case: Supports the sequence for checking the systemic condition. The stated temperature “up to 38°C” does not document the temperature threshold of classic fever of unknown origin; objective inflammatory markers still need explanation. This is not a specialized guideline on spondylodiscitis, abscess or laboratory error.

items.body: With clinical suspicion of giant cell arteritis, initial imaging may be expert ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries; the choice of alternative imaging depends on the region and availability. Strong suspicion with ischemic visual manifestations requires urgent clinical action without waiting for a planned study. Application to the case: Age 55 and inflammation allow clarifying relevant symptoms but do not establish vasculitis by themselves. items.body: ANA are an entry condition for lupus classification, not a standalone diagnosis. Clinical and immunological features without a better alternative explanation are needed; classification criteria do not replace diagnosis. The temperature criterion is above 38.3°C; with high C-reactive protein, infection must be considered. Application to the case: ANA 1:320 justifies an organ-directed assessment, but the method and specific manifestations are unknown. By the description of up to 38°C the temperature criterion is not met; this does not exclude lupus. Unknown organ results are not counted as negative.

items.body: The Still profile includes typical temperature spikes ≥39°C, a transient rash, musculoskeletal manifestations and inflammatory activity; arthritis is not mandatory. Infections, tumors and other inflammatory diseases need to be considered. In a rheumatic context, the combination of persistent fever, splenomegaly, rising ferritin, low cell counts, liver/coagulation abnormalities or triglycerides requires assessment for macrophage activation syndrome; any single feature is non-specific. Application to the case: A temperature up to 38°C does not match the typical description of spikes; rash, blood differential and ferritin are unknown. The section on macrophage activation syndrome signals a need to assess hyperinflammation but is not a full algorithm for secondary HLH in lymphoma or infection.

items.body: Drug fever requires temporal matching with exposure, assessment of other causes and the course after stopping the drug. The review uses a working definition with regression within 72 hours but notes that definitions vary. Re-challenge is not a safe universal confirmation. Application to the case: Meropenem and vancomycin document exposure but not its causation. The entire medication chronology is needed, including drugs before April; the available description does not establish the start date of each agent. The review does not replace a severe drug reaction protocol.

items.body: The working definition of selective IgA deficiency requires more than low IgA: clinical/family context, repeat IgA together with IgG and IgM, exclusion of secondary causes, a preserved IgG vaccine response and exclusion of a T-cell defect are considered. Application to the case: IgA 0.06 g/L is a reason to reassess immunoglobulins. A single undated result is insufficient. items.body: Criteria for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease require both major features: corresponding node histology and node enlargement in at least two regions; minor criteria and exclusion of mimics are also required. Inflammation, anemia and splenomegaly alone are insufficient; autoantibodies alone are not an exclusion. Application to the case: The historical alternative is kept separate from lymphoma. There is no full node assessment or histology, so the major criteria are unchecked rather than proven absent. The subtype is not established; the table is part 1 of 2 and is not used as a complete finished algorithm.

Alongside the version “Lymphoma as a possible explanation of prolonged fever and night sweats”, the following were considered: infective endocarditis, including culture-negative after antibiotics; tuberculosis, including extrapulmonary or disseminated; an occult local infectious focus: abscess or osteoarticular infection; large-vessel vasculitis, including giant cell arteritis; systemic autoimmune disease, including systemic lupus erythematosus; adult-onset Still disease as a conditional autoinflammatory alternative; drug-induced fever as a possible factor in its persistence; secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis as a conditional dangerous complication; IgA reduction: isolated deficiency or a broader humoral immunity disorder; a thyroid nodule and other possible concurrent CT findings; and incompleteness of the clinical chronology and laboratory conditions as a source of erroneous conclusions. Such a list did not imply equal probability of all conditions. Its function was different: not to lose a close morphological alternative, another mechanism, a potentially correctable cause, a separate parallel process or an error of the study itself.

emphasis_terms: Infective endocarditis or other endovascular infection
narrative.text: After comparing the clinical data with the sources, the leading working version became “Infective endocarditis or other endovascular infection”. Fever since April, night sweats, splenomegaly and prolonged inflammatory activity together support checking for an infectious source. Endocarditis is a specific dangerous treatable version; device or vascular catheter infection depends on a still unknown exposure. Recorded grounds of support: This feature is part of a shared pattern of fever, night sweats, splenomegaly and inflammation. The constellation justifies checking; individual components are not independent specific evidence. Clinical compatibility is shared by infections, lymphoma and non-infectious inflammation; current activity is unknown. Neutral context: Antibiotics could have affected the informativeness of microbiology; the source contains neither the cultures themselves nor the response to therapy. An undetermined cause of fever does not prove the absence of infection or treatment failure. Procalcitonin 0.06 ng/mL is kept as an undated result; it is not matched to the inflammation peak. Not used to exclude endocarditis or another local infection. The most important limitation was that the pattern is also compatible with lymphoma and non-infectious inflammation, endocarditis is not confirmed, and procalcitonin 0.06 ng/mL is undated; antibiotic exposure proves neither a bacterial cause nor its exclusion. The level of confidence could be definitively changed by blood cultures and their timing relative to antibiotics, and by valvular history, examination, echocardiography and devices/catheters.

The closest alternative remained “Lymphoma of undetermined subtype”. Prolonged systemic symptoms together with splenomegaly and hemoglobin 121 g/L support a hematological check. With splenic predominance and clonal small B cells, splenic marginal zone lymphoma and other mature B-cell neoplasms are clarified; with a nodal/tissue focus — Hodgkin lymphoma and aggressive B-cell lymphomas. These conditional branches are not established subtypes. Key limitation: mild splenomegaly and anemia do not prove splenic or bone marrow presentation, and LDH 410.8 U/L and β₂-microglobulin 2.28 mg/L without date or references do not determine subtype or priority. This version could be clarified by the full CT protocol, examination and course of spleen/nodes, a blood differential and smear with immunophenotyping if relevant cells are present, and a diagnostically adequate biopsy of the detected lesion. “Tuberculosis, including extrapulmonary” remains a diagnostic alternative without an established priority. Fever, night sweats and splenomegaly together allow for a chronic infection. Tuberculosis remains a specific alternative; nontuberculous mycobacteria and fungal infections require separate exposures, immune context and material. Key limitation: there are no data that currently separate this direction from other chronic infections and lymphoma, and a negative CMV PCR is not a tuberculosis test; the checked selection contains no specific sources for fungal and nontuberculous mycobacterial algorithms. This version could be clarified by contacts, travel, HIV status and immunosuppression, and by a focus with corresponding microbiology/histology. Comparing these versions shifted attention from the general similarity of manifestations to the specific result that would change the classification.

This version could be clarified by a temperature curve and examination during the episode, blood differential, ferritin and relevant organ values, and a check of infectious and tumor alternatives. Comparing these versions shifted attention from the general similarity of manifestations to the specific result that would change the classification.

Key limitation: exposure alone does not prove causation; the known description gives no exact drug start dates, and a temporal coincidence or improvement after therapy ends may have another explanation. Source support of the synthesis: 13. For each source the accepted statement and its applicability to the clinical question are given.

“JSH practical guidelines for hematological malignancies, 2023: II. lymphoma—overview”. Assessing suspected lymphoma combines a history of systemic symptoms, examination of nodes and spleen, a complete blood count with morphology and imaging. Diagnosis usually requires a biopsy of the relevant lesion before treatment. Applicability: Helps define how to check systemic symptoms and splenomegaly. Does not prove lymphoma or its subtype; the list of lymphoma workups does not make all invasive procedures mandatory in unexplained fever.

“NCCN Guidelines Version 4.2026: Splenic Marginal Zone Lymphoma”. Splenic marginal zone lymphoma requires morphological and immunophenotypic data. Some cases can be recognized by clonal small B cells in blood and/or bone marrow after excluding other small B-cell neoplasms. A negative PET-CT does not exclude marginal zone lymphoma. The workup for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma includes anatomical assessment of nodes and organs, blood differential, LDH and imaging. Bone marrow biopsy is listed among studies for selected cases; this section is not a way to establish a subtype from systemic symptoms alone. Applicability: Supports only a conditional branch with a corresponding cellular and anatomical pattern. Mild splenomegaly and hemoglobin 121 g/L do not by themselves indicate this subtype or justify splenectomy. Used to limit the historical branch of aggressive B-cell lymphoma: morphology of a suspicious focus is needed first. Staging and pre-treatment assessment studies are not automatically transferred to undiagnosed fever.

“NCCN Guidelines Version 2.2026: Hodgkin Lymphoma”. If Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected, a diagnostically adequate node biopsy, usually excisional, is preferred; fine-needle aspiration alone is usually insufficient. FDG uptake may be infectious or inflammatory and needs clinical or pathological clarification. Applicability: Applicable once a suitable focus for biopsy appears. The available temperature up to 38°C and night sweats do not automatically warrant attributing the formal B-symptom complex or a Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis.

“Blood Culture–Negative Endocarditis: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association”. Antibiotics before blood collection are a common cause of negative cultures in endocarditis. With clinical suspicion, proper culture sets and valve assessment are needed; further pathogen search depends on exposures, prior antibiotics and primary results. Negative cultures after antibiotics do not exclude infection. Applicability: Clarifies the meaning of the known antibiotic exposure and the missing cultures/echocardiography. The time of intake and blood collection are unknown; there are no culture results, so calling the case proven culture-negative endocarditis is premature. The source does not justify exclusion by procalcitonin.

“Official American Thoracic Society/Infectious Diseases Society of America/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children”. IGRA and the tuberculin test do not distinguish latent infection from active tuberculosis. If an extrapulmonary process is suspected, material from the relevant focus is examined: culture, molecular methods and, if indicated, histology. Negative results of a single test may not exclude disease. Applicability: Allows choosing a check once a contact or focus is established. There is currently no material, exposures or tuberculosis tests; this is not a recommendation for invasive sampling without a clinical target.

“EANM consensus document on the use of [18F]FDG PET/CT in fever and inflammation of unknown origin”. Unexplained fever and unexplained inflammation have infectious, non-infectious inflammatory, neoplastic and other causes. The initial assessment includes history, examination, a blood count with differential and inflammatory markers. FDG PET-CT may localize a focus for a directed check after a non-diagnostic initial workup; FDG uptake does not determine etiology. Applicability: Supports the sequence for checking the systemic condition. The stated temperature “up to 38°C” does not document the temperature threshold of classic fever of unknown origin; objective inflammatory markers still need explanation. This is not a specialized guideline on spondylodiscitis, abscess or laboratory error.

“EULAR recommendations for the use of imaging in large vessel vasculitis in clinical practice: 2023 update.”. With clinical suspicion of giant cell arteritis, initial imaging may be expert ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries; the choice of alternative imaging depends on the region and availability. Strong suspicion with ischemic visual manifestations requires urgent clinical action without waiting for a planned study. Applicability: Age 55 and inflammation allow clarifying relevant symptoms but do not establish vasculitis by themselves. Clinical suspicion, operator experience and the effect of glucocorticoids already received change the interpretation of results; no treatment is prescribed here.

“2019 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus”. ANA are an entry condition for lupus classification, not a standalone diagnosis. Clinical and immunological features without a better alternative explanation are needed; classification criteria do not replace diagnosis. The temperature criterion is above 38.3°C; with high C-reactive protein, infection must be considered. Applicability: ANA 1:320 justifies an organ-directed assessment, but the method and specific manifestations are unknown. By the description of up to 38°C the temperature criterion is not met; this does not exclude lupus. Unknown organ results are not counted as negative.

“EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still’s disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still’s disease”. The Still profile includes typical temperature spikes ≥39°C, a transient rash, musculoskeletal manifestations and inflammatory activity; arthritis is not mandatory. Infections, tumors and other inflammatory diseases need to be considered. In a rheumatic context, the combination of persistent fever, splenomegaly, rising ferritin, low cell counts, liver/coagulation abnormalities or triglycerides requires assessment for macrophage activation syndrome; any single feature is non-specific. Applicability: A temperature up to 38°C does not match the typical description of spikes; rash, blood differential and ferritin are unknown. The section on macrophage activation syndrome signals a need to assess hyperinflammation but is not a full algorithm for secondary HLH in lymphoma or infection.

“Drug fever: a narrative review”. Drug fever requires temporal matching with exposure, assessment of other causes and the course after stopping the drug. The review uses a working definition with regression within 72 hours but notes that definitions vary. Re-challenge is not a safe universal confirmation. Applicability: Meropenem and vancomycin document exposure but not its causation. The entire medication chronology is needed, including drugs before April; the available description does not establish the start date of each agent. The review does not replace a severe drug reaction protocol.

“ESID Registry – Working Definitions for Clinical Diagnosis of PID, November 2019”. The working definition of selective IgA deficiency requires more than low IgA: clinical/family context, repeat IgA together with IgG and IgM, exclusion of secondary causes, a preserved IgG vaccine response and exclusion of a T-cell defect are considered. Applicability: IgA 0.06 g/L is a reason to reassess immunoglobulins. A single undated result is insufficient. The page does not contain the full CVID criteria pathway, so this diagnosis is not established.

“2023 European Thyroid Association Clinical Practice Guidelines for thyroid nodule management”. The initial assessment of a thyroid nodule includes history, examination, TSH and neck ultrasound. The need for puncture is determined after clinical, functional and ultrasound assessment, taking risk and size into account. Applicability: Applicable to the described left nodule. Size, ultrasound features and TSH are unknown; no automatic puncture or causal link to the fever is established. Exact thresholds from the tables were not used.

“NCCN Guidelines Version 2.2026: Castleman Disease”. Criteria for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease require both major features: corresponding node histology and node enlargement in at least two regions; minor criteria and exclusion of mimics are also required. Inflammation, anemia and splenomegaly alone are insufficient; autoantibodies alone are not an exclusion. Applicability: The historical alternative is kept separate from lymphoma. There is no full node assessment or histology, so the major criteria are unchecked rather than proven absent. The subtype is not established; the table is part 1 of 2 and is not used as a complete finished algorithm.

After ranking, the uncertainty could already be formulated as specific clinical questions. The first remaining question was what the current symptoms and inflammatory markers are after the last dates given; it mattered because without this, current activity and urgency are not determined; old values are not today's state. The second remaining question was what the cultures, echocardiography and local search showed and when antibiotics were given; it mattered because the absence of results does not mean a negative workup or ineffective treatment. The third remaining question was whether there is a nodule, tissue lesion or clonal cells suitable for verification; it mattered because the available description does not define the distribution of involvement; the lymphoma subtype and Castleman major criteria remain unestablished. The fourth remaining question was which primary forms confirm the units, references, methods and timing of all values; it mattered because biochemistry without units does not allow conclusions about normal organ function; undated tests cannot be considered simultaneous with the inflammation peak. The fifth remaining question was whether there are vascular, autoimmune or autoinflammatory clinical signs; it mattered because absence of a description is not equivalent to absence on examination; the phenotype itself will set the order of targeted tests. The sixth remaining question was whether there is sufficient specialized support for a specific infectious focus and the wider infectious series; it mattered because the checked literature gives a general localization pathway and a tuberculosis pathway. Full algorithms for abscess/spondylodiscitis, nontuberculous mycobacteria and fungal infections are missing; if relevant signs appear, a targeted specialist review is needed. The next remaining question was whether there are current criteria data and specialized justification for secondary HLH if infection or lymphoma is suspected; it mattered because the available support on MAS is rheumatological; it cannot be presented as a complete algorithm for other causes. The next remaining question was whether the IgA reduction is persistent and what the full immunoglobulin profile is; it mattered because the working criteria for selective deficiency are not met by the available data; CVID needs a separate full assessment. In this form the gap ceased to be an abstract lack of information and became a testable condition for changing the diagnostic conclusion.

In summary, the available data were sufficient for a responsible working candidate, but not for a final diagnosis. There is sufficient material for a working differential conclusion with early infectious and hematological checks. An endovascular infectious source is checked first, the lymphoma direction starts in parallel; this is a workup sequence, not a probability estimate. Current activity, etiology and subtype are not yet established. Therefore, at this stage the protocol did not allow establishing the final diagnosis or lymphoma subtype, prescribing treatment, performing an invasive procedure without a clinical target, or using old results as the current state; these decisions remained dependent on new data and the clinician's assessment.

Scientific statements were checked only in the retained exact fragments. Specialized algorithms for abscess/spondylodiscitis, fungal/nontuberculous mycobacterial infections, general secondary HLH and CVID are incompletely covered; they are not presented as a completed check. No quantitative conclusions were made for biochemistry without units; exact source values and unknown dates are kept. Priorities are a clinical order of checking, not calibrated probabilities. This conclusion creates no clinician acceptance or prescriptions. This record marked the point where the evidential force of the available data ended and the zone of decisions after new material began.

Further progress depended on results capable of changing the classification: a current examination, temperature curve, tests and an exact treatment chronology; and cultures/echocardiography if infection is suspected, a full CT, cellular blood assessment and a target for verification. source_library.applicability: Helps define how to check systemic symptoms and splenomegaly. Does not prove lymphoma or its subtype; the list of lymphoma workups does not make all invasive procedures mandatory in unexplained fever.
source_library.proposition: Assessing suspected lymphoma combines a history of systemic symptoms, examination of nodes and spleen, a complete blood count with morphology and imaging. Diagnosis usually requires a biopsy of the relevant lesion before treatment.
source_library.title: JSH practical guidelines for hematological malignancies, 2023: II. lymphoma—overview

source_library.applicability: Supports only a conditional branch with a corresponding cellular and anatomical pattern. Mild splenomegaly and hemoglobin 121 g/L do not by themselves indicate this subtype or justify splenectomy. Used to limit the historical branch of aggressive B-cell lymphoma: morphology of a suspicious focus is needed first. Staging and pre-treatment assessment studies are not automatically transferred to undiagnosed fever.
source_library.proposition: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma requires morphological and immunophenotypic data. Some cases can be recognized by clonal small B cells in blood and/or bone marrow after excluding other small B-cell neoplasms. A negative PET-CT does not exclude marginal zone lymphoma. The workup for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma includes anatomical assessment of nodes and organs, blood differential, LDH and imaging. Bone marrow biopsy is listed among studies for selected cases; this section is not a way to establish a subtype from systemic symptoms alone.
source_library.title: NCCN Guidelines Version 4.2026: Splenic Marginal Zone Lymphoma

source_library.applicability: Applicable once a suitable focus for biopsy appears. The available temperature up to 38°C and night sweats do not automatically warrant attributing the formal B-symptom complex or a Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis.
source_library.proposition: If Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected, a diagnostically adequate node biopsy, usually excisional, is preferred; fine-needle aspiration alone is usually insufficient. FDG uptake may be infectious or inflammatory and needs clinical or pathological clarification.
source_library.title: NCCN Guidelines Version 2.2026: Hodgkin Lymphoma

source_library.applicability: Clarifies the meaning of the known antibiotic exposure and the missing cultures/echocardiography. The time of intake and blood collection are unknown; there are no culture results, so calling the case proven culture-negative endocarditis is premature. The source does not justify exclusion by procalcitonin.
source_library.location: Paragraph-only full-body derivative; exact source XML retained. Tables, figures and supplementary material excluded.
source_library.proposition: Antibiotics before blood collection are a common cause of negative cultures in endocarditis. With clinical suspicion, proper culture sets and valve assessment are needed; further pathogen search depends on exposures, prior antibiotics and primary results. Negative cultures after antibiotics do not exclude infection.
source_library.title: Blood Culture–Negative Endocarditis: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association

source_library.applicability: Allows choosing a check once a contact or focus is established. There is currently no material, exposures or tuberculosis tests; this is not a recommendation for invasive sampling without a clinical target.
source_library.location: Prose-only full text; exact BioC source retained
source_library.proposition: IGRA and the tuberculin test do not distinguish latent infection from active tuberculosis. If an extrapulmonary process is suspected, material from the relevant focus is examined: culture, molecular methods and, if indicated, histology. Negative results of a single test may not exclude disease.
source_library.title: Official American Thoracic Society/Infectious Diseases Society of America/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children

source_library.applicability: Supports the sequence for checking the systemic condition. The stated temperature “up to 38°C” does not document the temperature threshold of classic fever of unknown origin; objective inflammatory markers still need explanation. This is not a specialized guideline on spondylodiscitis, abscess or laboratory error.
source_library.location: Prose-only full text; exact BioC source retained
source_library.proposition: Unexplained fever and unexplained inflammation have infectious, non-infectious inflammatory, neoplastic and other causes. The initial assessment includes history, examination, a blood count with differential and inflammatory markers. FDG PET-CT may localize a focus for a directed check after a non-diagnostic initial workup; FDG uptake does not determine etiology.
source_library.title: EANM consensus document on the use of [18F]FDG PET/CT in fever and inflammation of unknown origin

source_library.applicability: Age 55 and inflammation allow clarifying relevant symptoms but do not establish vasculitis by themselves. Clinical suspicion, operator experience and the effect of glucocorticoids already received change the interpretation of results; no treatment is prescribed here.
source_library.location: Official publisher HTML text; use overarching principles and Recommendation 1-3 prose only, no protocol table/image claims.
source_library.proposition: With clinical suspicion of giant cell arteritis, initial imaging may be expert ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries; the choice of alternative imaging depends on the region and availability. Strong suspicion with ischemic visual manifestations requires urgent clinical action without waiting for a planned study.
source_library.title: EULAR recommendations for the use of imaging in large vessel vasculitis in clinical practice: 2023 update.

source_library.applicability: ANA 1:320 justifies an organ-directed assessment, but the method and specific manifestations are unknown. By the description of up to 38°C the temperature criterion is not met; this does not exclude lupus. Unknown organ results are not counted as negative.
source_library.location: Physical PDF pages 5, 7, 8: clinical definitions, final classification criteria, discussion
source_library.proposition: ANA are an entry condition for lupus classification, not a standalone diagnosis. Clinical and immunological features without a better alternative explanation are needed; classification criteria do not replace diagnosis. The temperature criterion is above 38.3°C; with high C-reactive protein, infection must be considered.
source_library.title: 2019 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus

source_library.applicability: A temperature up to 38°C does not match the typical description of spikes; rash, blood differential and ferritin are unknown. The section on macrophage activation syndrome signals a need to assess hyperinflammation but is not a full algorithm for secondary HLH in lymphoma or infection.
source_library.location: Paragraph-only full-body derivative; exact source XML retained. Tables, figures and supplementary material excluded.
source_library.proposition: The Still profile includes typical temperature spikes ≥39°C, a transient rash, musculoskeletal manifestations and inflammatory activity; arthritis is not mandatory. Infections, tumors and other inflammatory diseases need to be considered. In a rheumatic context, the combination of persistent fever, splenomegaly, rising ferritin, low cell counts, liver/coagulation abnormalities or triglycerides requires assessment for macrophage activation syndrome; any single feature is non-specific.
source_library.title: EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still’s disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still’s disease

source_library.applicability: Meropenem and vancomycin document exposure but not its causation. The review does not replace a severe drug reaction protocol.
source_library.location: Body prose: definition, clinical presentation and diagnosis; tables excluded
source_library.proposition: Drug fever requires temporal matching with exposure, assessment of other causes and the course after stopping the drug. The review uses a working definition with regression within 72 hours but notes that definitions vary. Re-challenge is not a safe universal confirmation.
source_library.title: Drug fever: a narrative review

source_library.applicability: IgA 0.06 g/L is a reason to reassess immunoglobulins. A single undated result is insufficient. The page does not contain the full CVID criteria pathway, so this diagnosis is not established.
source_library.proposition: The working definition of selective IgA deficiency requires more than low IgA: clinical/family context, repeat IgA together with IgG and IgM, exclusion of secondary causes, a preserved IgG vaccine response and exclusion of a T-cell defect are considered.
source_library.title: ESID Registry – Working Definitions for Clinical Diagnosis of PID, November 2019

source_library.applicability: Applicable to the described left nodule. Size, ultrasound features and TSH are unknown; no automatic puncture or causal link to the fever is established. Exact thresholds from the tables were not used.
source_library.location: Body prose: initial evaluation, clinical and laboratory evaluation, ultrasound; tables/figures excluded
source_library.proposition: The initial assessment of a thyroid nodule includes history, examination, TSH and neck ultrasound. The need for puncture is determined after clinical, functional and ultrasound assessment, taking risk and size into account.
source_library.title: 2023 European Thyroid Association Clinical Practice Guidelines for thyroid nodule management

source_library.applicability: The historical alternative is kept separate from lymphoma. There is no full node assessment or histology, so the major criteria are unchecked rather than proven absent. source_library.proposition: Criteria for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease require both major features: corresponding node histology and node enlargement in at least two regions; minor criteria and exclusion of mimics are also required. Inflammation, anemia and splenomegaly alone are insufficient; autoantibodies alone are not an exclusion.
source_library.title: NCCN Guidelines Version 2.2026: Castleman Disease

problem_representation.text: Male, 55 years. Since April 2026, fever of unknown origin with temperature up to 38°C and night sweats have been described. CT of 16.04.2026 — mild splenomegaly.
